svg.font-family: ui-sans-serif, system-ui, -apple-system, "Segoe UI", Roboto, "Helvetica Neue", Arial, sans-serif
svg.title: How onetree works: several coding agents in one git working tree
svg.desc: Animated diagram of onetree. Three coding agents share one git working tree. Each has a private index, claims the files it will write, and lands through a commit broker that audits the claims, runs a payload gate and the test suite, and then moves the branch. The animation has seven steps. Step 1: Each agent registers a session and gets its own git index. Staging is private; the working tree is shared. Three agent cards (Agent A, Agent B, Agent C) stand on the left. In the middle is a panel titled "One shared working tree" with five files. On the right are the commit broker and the branch main. A box labelled "index" appears inside each agent card: each session has registered and received its own private git index. Three session_register events appear in the event log at the bottom. Step 2: Before editing, a session claims the exact paths it will write. A claim is an exclusive lease on a path. Agent A claims src/api.py, Agent B claims src/auth.py and Agent C claims tests/test_api.py. An arrow runs from each agent to its file, and the file row shows "claimed by A" (or B, or C) with a badge carrying the agent's letter. Three claim events are appended to the log. Step 3: A claim on a held path is refused, and the refusal names the holder. A change to a path you did not claim cannot land. Agent C also asks for src/api.py, which Agent A holds. The request is refused: the row shows "C refused: held by A" and a crossed-out badge with the letter C. A refused event is appended to the log. Step 4: Agents edit their claimed files in the one working tree and stage them with ordinary git, each into its own index. Each agent edits its own file in the shared working tree; the rows change to "edited by A", "edited by B" and "edited by C". Each agent then stages its file into its own index: the index box in each agent card now names the staged file. Step 5: onetree land audits the claims, runs the admitted payload gate and your tests, then moves the branch ref by compare-and-swap. Agent A lands. A chip labelled "candidate A" travels from A's index to the commit broker. The broker's four steps turn green one after another: claims audit, payload gate, test referee, compare-and-swap. A new commit marked A appears on the branch main, the file row shows "landed by A", and the events land_intent and landed are appended to the log. Step 6: If the tests fail on the candidate, the landing is refused. The branch does not move, and the refusal is recorded. Agent B tries to land. Its candidate passes the claims audit and the payload gate, but the test referee turns red: the tests fail on the candidate. The candidate is marked refused, a crossed-out circle shows that no commit was added to main, and a refused event is appended to the log. Step 7: One clone, one working tree, one linear history. Every claim, landing and refusal is an event in an append-only log kept in git: refs/onetree/wal. Agent C lands the same way as A: four green steps, and a second new commit, marked C, on main. The final picture: three agents, one working tree, a linear branch carrying the commits of A and C, B's change still waiting in the tree, and an event log with twelve entries.

g.text: 1 · Sessions: a private index for every agent
Each agent registers a session and gets its own git index.
Staging is private; the working tree is shared.
2 · Claims: exclusive write leases on paths
Before editing, a session claims the exact paths it will write.
A claim is an exclusive lease on a path.
A claim on a held path is refused, and the refusal names the holder.
A change to a path you did not claim cannot land.
4 · Edit in the shared tree, stage privately
Agents edit their claimed files in the one working tree and stage them
with ordinary git, each into its own index.
5 · Landing: every change goes through the broker
onetree land audits the claims, runs the admitted payload gate and your tests,
then moves the branch ref by compare-and-swap.
If the tests fail on the candidate, the landing is refused.
The branch does not move, and the refusal is recorded.
One clone, one working tree, one linear history. Every claim, landing and refusal
is an event in an append-only log kept in git: refs/onetree/wal.
